profile.reading: This building is one of three data centers on Vantage Data Centers' Quincy, Washington campus at 2101 M Street NE, in Grant County on the Columbia River plateau. Vantage entered the Quincy market for the same reason Microsoft, Yahoo, Sabey, and Intuit built there: Grant County Public Utility District sells some of the lowest-cost hydroelectric power in the continental United States, generated at the Wanapum and Priest Rapids dams on the Columbia River. The full Quincy campus covers roughly 68 acres and totals about 775,000 square feet across its three buildings, with a combined critical IT load Vantage has stated at approximately 89 megawatts. Vantage's own campus materials individually name WA11, citing Uptime Institute Tier III Design and Constructed certification, Tier III Gold Operational Sustainability status, and LEED Gold; the operator's public materials do not similarly break out WA12 and WA13 by name, certification, or individual square footage and megawatt figures, so this facility's specifications should be read as part of the shared campus totals rather than an individually confirmed number for this specific building. Standard design follows Vantage's N+1 mechanical redundancy approach, with diesel backup generators meeting current EPA Tier II emissions standards, and the region's cool, dry high-desert climate supports substantial use of outside-air economization for cooling, reducing water and mechanical-cooling load relative to humid-climate sites. Grant County's concentration of hyperscale and colocation data centers has drawn periodic public scrutiny over discounted industrial electricity rates for large users relative to residential ratepayers, a recurring topic at Grant County PUD commissioner meetings and in Washington state legislative discussions of data center power consumption and grid capacity. Quincy's data center campuses sit within land the city and county have zoned for industrial and manufacturing use, and local officials have continued to permit sector growth given its role as a major employer and property-tax contributor in a city of roughly 8,000 residents.

reading.body:
Vantage WA13 is one of three buildings on the Vantage Quincy campus in Grant County, Washington, a site chosen for access to hydroelectric power from the Columbia River dams at costs among the lowest in the continental United States. The full campus totals 89 megawatts of critical IT load and 775,000 square feet across all three buildings, but individual specifications for WA13 alone are not published separately. The campus sits within industrial-zoned land 68 acres in area, alongside other hyperscale data centers built for the same power advantage, in a county where discounted electricity rates for large users have drawn ongoing public scrutiny.

The Quincy campus design follows Vantage's N+1 mechanical redundancy standard with diesel backup generators meeting EPA Tier II emissions standards. The region's high-desert climate enables substantial outside-air economization for cooling, reducing water and mechanical load compared to humid sites. WA11, one of the three campus buildings, holds Uptime Institute Tier III Design and Constructed certification, Tier III Gold Operational Sustainability status, and LEED Gold, though Vantage does not publish equivalent certifications separately for WA12 and WA13.

This campus represents the third-largest published megawatt capacity in Washington state, behind only two other facilities, and ranks among 46 mapped data center facilities in the state, of which only two others have published power specifications. The Quincy site matters to AI scaling primarily as part of a regional power arbitrage: Grant County's concentration of hyperscale capacity is bound by the fixed hydroelectric output of two dams and the ability of the local utility district to sustain discounted rates for industrial users, a constraint that will tighten as more capacity comes online.
